subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage: At the birthday party in Leeds, two-year-old Chidi raced laps around the sofa, shrieking with laughter and rubbing his eyes. "He's full of beans!" someone said. Clara, his aunt, watched him trip over a balloon and burst into loud sobs. She scooped him up. "Not beans," she murmured. "You're done in." His eyes were red. She carried him to the quiet bedroom, drew the curtains and lay beside him. He was asleep before the second song.

qa.q: What did Chidi trip over?
qa.a: A balloon.

qa.q: What did Clara think was really going on while Chidi raced and shrieked?
qa.a: She thought he was overtired rather than just excited; the eye-rubbing and sudden sobs told her he needed sleep.

qa.q: What small step helped Chidi settle?
qa.a: Clara took him to a quiet bedroom, drew the curtains and lay beside him, giving his tired body a calm place to sleep.

qa.q: What was the party like for Chidi by the time he tripped?
qa.a: It was probably too much for him; he was so worn out that a small fall tipped his loud laughter straight into tears.

grounding: Illustrates an adult reading a toddler's wild, loud play and eye-rubbing as a sign that sleep is overdue.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage: Most evenings I, Sharmila, sit on the bench by our building's swings. Last Thursday, little Varun from the ground floor was everywhere at once: climbing the slide the wrong way, laughing far too loudly, rubbing his eyes with both fists. "Sharmila aunty, catch me!" he yelled, then flopped onto the sand and howled when his slipper came off. His mother frowned. "Stop this drama." I said, "Maybe he's sleepy?" She looked at his droopy eyelids and carried him home.

qa.q: What did Varun do when his slipper came off?
qa.a: He flopped onto the sand and howled.

qa.q: What was Varun's mother feeling at first, and what changed her mind?
qa.a: She felt irritated and read it as drama; after Sharmila's comment, his droopy eyelids showed her he was tired.

qa.q: What small step helped here?
qa.a: Sharmila gently suggested he might be sleepy instead of joining the scolding, and his mother took him home to rest.

qa.q: How might the evening have felt for Varun?
qa.a: Probably overwhelming; his body was worn out, so he could not slow down, and a lost slipper felt huge.

grounding: Shows a neighbour noticing that a toddler's loud, wild play and eye-rubbing point to overdue sleep rather than misbehaviour.

Friday: Kunal raced round the sofa at nine, shrieking with laughter. Pooja scolded him when he knocked over the lamp, and he burst into tears.
Saturday: The same wild laughing. This time Pooja watched closely. Between laps he rubbed his eyes and yawned mid-giggle.
Sunday: At the very first eye-rub, Pooja switched off the TV and dimmed the lights. Kunal protested, then flopped onto her lap, asleep in minutes.

qa.q: What did Kunal knock over on Friday?
qa.a: He knocked over the lamp.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt about Friday once she noticed the eye-rubbing?
qa.a: She may have felt a little guilty for scolding, once she saw that the wild laughing meant he was overtired rather than naughty.

qa.q: What small step did Pooja take on Sunday?
qa.a: At the first eye-rub she switched off the TV and dimmed the lights, catching his tiredness before the wild stage.

qa.q: What is it like for Kunal when he is scolded on Friday?
qa.a: He is exhausted and confused, and the scolding tips him straight from laughter into tears.

grounding: Shows an adult learning that a toddler's wild laughing and running were signs that bedtime was overdue, not misbehaviour.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage: At the Kothrud daycare, Wasim was zooming between the cots at two o'clock, laughing so loudly that the helper frowned. "That one is being naughty again," she said. Rajni watched a little longer. His eyes were pink, and between laps he kept rubbing them with his fists. When he tripped on a cushion, the laughter turned into wailing in a second. Rajni picked him up and carried him to the corner mat under the slow fan. "Not naughty. Sleepy," she told the helper. He was snoring before she finished humming.

qa.q: What time was Wasim zooming between the cots?
qa.a: At two o'clock.

qa.q: What made Rajni look past the helper's view?
qa.a: She was curious and concerned, so she watched longer and noticed his pink eyes and the constant rubbing.

qa.q: What would you advise the helper the next time a child gets wild at nap time?
qa.a: Look for rubbed eyes and a sudden switch to tears, and move the child somewhere dim and calm instead of scolding.

qa.q: How does the helper see Wasim at first?
qa.a: The helper sees a naughty child being loud, missing that he is overtired and needs his nap.

grounding: Shows a daycare worker reading a toddler's hyper laughing and eye-rubbing as an overdue nap rather than misbehaviour.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage:
"Alka, look, so much energy at nine o'clock!"
"Vidya, that's not energy. Watch his eyes."
"Chintu, catch me!"
"See him rubbing them? That laugh is too loud. It's his overtired laugh."
"He's bouncing off the walls!"
"Exactly. Wait."
A thump. A wail.
"Oh no, he fell over nothing and now he's sobbing."
"Every time. Can you switch off the big light?"
"Sorry, I thought I was helping."
"You're a lovely masi. Come, Chintu, song time."

qa.q: What does Alka ask Vidya to switch off?
qa.a: The big light.

qa.q: How does Alka feel when Chintu gets wild at nine?
qa.a: She is calm and knowing, because she recognises his overtired laugh and expects the crash before it comes.

qa.q: What could Vidya do differently next time Chintu laughs wildly at night?
qa.a: Watch for the eye-rubbing and the too-loud laugh, skip the chase game, and help dim the lights for bedtime.

qa.q: Why might Vidya read Chintu's laughing differently from Alka?
qa.a: As a visiting masi, Vidya sees a happy, lively child and does not yet know his signs of being overtired.

grounding: Shows a caregiver recognising that a toddler's loud laughing and running at night mean he is overtired, while a visitor mistakes it for energy.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage:
Daycare note for Siddharth's parents
At four, Siddharth was racing laps round the room, shrieking with laughter and knocking over the block tower. It looked like fun, but he was rubbing his eyes between laps. My colleague wanted to put him in time-out. I thought he was overtired, not naughty. I dimmed the lights and sat with him on the mat with his soft rabbit. Two minutes later he burst into tears, then fell asleep on my lap. He had skipped his nap today.
Kiran

qa.q: What did Kiran notice Siddharth doing between laps?
qa.a: Rubbing his eyes.

qa.q: Why did Kiran decide against time-out?
qa.a: Kiran felt concerned that Siddharth was overtired, not naughty, and wanted him to rest rather than be punished.

qa.q: What did Kiran do instead?
qa.a: Dimmed the lights and sat with Siddharth on the mat with his soft rabbit until he could fall asleep.

qa.q: What was the wild running like for Siddharth?
qa.a: He was probably so tired he couldn't settle, so the laughter tipped into tears once the room calmed.

grounding: A carer reads a toddler's wild, loud play as a sign that a nap is overdue rather than misbehaviour.
